holidays.name: National Nothing Day
holidays.description: A day dedicated to doing absolutely nothing. No parades, no celebrations, no activism, just sitting around and savoring the glorious void of obligation.
holidays.origin: Created by journalist Harold Pullman Coffin in 1972 as a day when Americans could just sit without celebrating or protesting anything. It was officially recognized by the National Observance community and was often observed on the third Monday of January in later years.
holidays.funFact: Harold Coffin's goal was to give Americans one day to just sit without honoring, observing, or celebrating anything, and the day was famously promoted in newspapers during the 1970s.

holidays.name: National Hot and Spicy Food Day
holidays.description: A fiery celebration for anyone who loves their meals with a kick. Folks dare each other to try hotter sauces, spicier curries, and peppers that bring on happy tears.
holidays.origin: A food-industry-style observance that grew from the popularity of spicy cuisines, such as Mexican, Thai, Indian, and Szechuan, and the rise of hot sauce culture in the United States.
holidays.funFact: The heat of chili peppers is measured on the Scoville scale, and the Carolina Reaper pepper has been measured at over 1.6 million Scoville heat units, roughly 200 times hotter than a jalapeño.

holidays.name: International Hot and Spicy Food Day
holidays.description: A global spicy food celebration where people around the world spice up their plates, from fiery curries to blazing hot wings, and test their tolerance for heat.
holidays.origin: This observance emerged from hot and spicy food enthusiasts and promoters of spicy cuisine, and it is celebrated informally on January 16 each year by restaurants and foodies.
holidays.funFact: Capsaicin, the compound that makes peppers hot, tricks your brain into thinking your mouth is burning, and mammals feel it while birds do not, which is why birds spread pepper seeds without a care.

holidays.name: Appreciate a Dragon Day
holidays.description: A day to honor dragons, from the majestic fire-breathers of fantasy novels to the wise serpentine dragons of Eastern legends. Fans celebrate with art, movie marathons, and dragon-themed snacks.
holidays.origin: Popularized by fantasy fans and pop culture enthusiasts, and often linked to the love of authors such as Tolkien, Anne McCaffrey, and the creators of How to Train Your Dragon and Game of Thrones.
holidays.funFact: Dragon legends appear on nearly every continent, and in Chinese culture dragons symbolize luck and power, while in many European myths they are fearsome hoarders of treasure.

holidays.name: Religious Freedom Day
holidays.description: An official US observance commemorating the freedom to practice any religion, or none at all, without government interference.
holidays.origin: Proclaimed annually by US presidents since 1993 to mark the anniversary of the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, which was drafted by Thomas Jefferson and passed on January 16, 1786.
holidays.funFact: Thomas Jefferson was so proud of writing the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom that he asked for it to be listed on his tombstone, and he left off being US President.
